Environmental Nanotechnology, Monitoring & Management

Volume 15, May 2021, 100409

E-waste management: A review of recycling process, environmental and occupational health hazards, and potential solutions

Author links open overlay panel,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enmm.2020.100409Get rights and content

Highlights

  • •

    An overview of the global e-waste generation and management is presented.

  • •

    Opportunities and constraints in e-waste management via recycling are discussed.

  • •

    Environmental and public health concerns due to unsafe recycling practices are discussed.

  • •

    Strategies to make e-waste recycling efficient and safer are suggested.

Abstract

The exponential growth in electronic waste (e-waste) comprising end-of-life electrical and electronic equipment has emerged as a major environmental concern. E-waste recycling, which comprises systematic collection of e-waste and its treatment for recycling of useful materials, offers a valuable tool to minimize the escalating heap of e-waste, supplement the shortage of some primary resources and support the economy. However, depending on the processing methods used for recycling, e-waste can also be a source of toxic substances, such as heavy metals, and persistent organic pollutants, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), brominated flame retardants (BFRs), perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins (PCDDs) and polychlorinated dibenzofurans (PCDFs). To efficiently harness the benefits of e-waste recycling without jeopardizing public health, a holistic approach encompassing improved product design and recycling rate and minimal emission of hazardous e-waste pollutants to the environment is required. In this review, we discuss the opportunities and constraints, and strategies for improved e-waste management. Further, we highlight the recent global trend in e-waste generation and provide an overview of the e-waste recycling process and the impact of e-waste pollutants on human health. Finally, a few strategies that can be implemented to make e-waste recycling an efficient and safer process have been discussed.

1. Introduction

Electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) such as cell phones, computers, video recorders, televisions, coffee machines, refrigerators and medical devices that add ease, comfort, and luxury to the modern life have become an indispensable part of modern societies. However, short lifespan, limited repair options and fast-changing technology is turning a high proportion of electronic gadgets into waste upon the end of its usable life due to damage, non-working, operational risks, or availability of better alternatives (Montalvo et al., 2016). Waste EEE (e-waste), mostly defined as “electrical or electronic equipment which is waste including all components, sub-assemblies and consumables, which are part of the product at the time of discarding” (Directive, 2008) have emerged both as a global concern due to its massively high volume and health hazards associated with its improper handling, disposal, or recycling (Forti et al., 2020; Grant et al., 2013; Widmer et al., 2005), as well as an opportunity due to high content of extractable valuable materials. Recent reports on global e-waste statistics have estimated global generation of 53.6 million ton (Mt) e-waste during 2019 that grew from 41.8 Mt in 2014 and 44.7 Mt in 2016 with further projection to grow to 74.7 Mt by 2030 at an annual growth rate of approx. 2 Mt (Balde et al., 2017, 2015; Forti et al., 2020).

E-waste generated at the household level in most of the countries is managed in three ways: (i) by dumping it to waste bins, (ii) through formal collection by government recognized bodies, and (iii) collection outside the formal system by individual waste dealers and companies (Chi et al., 2014). E-waste collected through authorized commercial and/or municipal collection points and pick-up services is usually recycled at facilities having advanced technology and machinery and infrastructure for safe and efficient removal of valuable materials (formal recycling). On the other hand, the e-waste collected outside the formal system by individual waste companies or dealers is mostly processed and recycled under sub-optimal conditions with primitive techniques and usually without any provisions to reduce the emission of hazardous chemicals into the environment (informal recycling) (Chi et al., 2011; Pradhan and Kumar, 2014). E-waste dumped into landfills or sold to peddlers often end up by polluting the environment through leaching into soil and groundwater, and via emission into the surrounding air, soil, and surface water (Cesaro et al., 2019; Man et al., 2013). A substantial amount of valuable resources are also lost through disposing or during recycling under inferior conditions. Thus, formal e-waste recycling is the safest way to manage e-waste. However, recent estimates suggest that only about 17.4 % (9.3 Mt) of the global e-waste generated in 2019 has been collected and recycled in the formal sector, leaving the flow of rest 44.3 Mt (82.6 %) e-waste undocumented (Forti et al., 2020). This suggests that most of the e-waste, particularly in Asian and African countries is managed by the informal sector. Presence of multiple precious metals (e.g. gold, platinum, palladium, ruthenium, rhodium, iridium, copper, and silver) along with other valuable materials such as iron, aluminium, cobalt, indium, germanium, bismuth, and antimony, make e-waste an attractive source of economy among local scrap dealers, dismantlers and recyclers (Deubzer et al., 2019). Toxic substances present in EEE (e.g. heavy metals, brominated flame retardants, and polychlorinated biphenyls), or those produced during recycling activities (e.g. polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and polychlorinated dibenzofurans), and used for extracting metals (e.g. acids like HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, HClO4, NaClO) are often emitted in the local environment as primary, secondary and tertiary emissions, respectively from informal recycling, leading to an increase in the levels of toxic pollutants in the ecosystem (Kumar et al., 2019; Orlins and Guan, 2016; Quan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015). Long term recycling activities in the informal sector compounded with long term persistence of e-waste pollutant in the environment increases the exposure risk to the waste recycling workers and the population inhabiting nearby localities and thus is a health hazard (Grant et al., 2013).

To establish a balance between the negative impact of e-waste recycling on the environment and human health, and resource reimbursement (financial), a multi-directional approach is required to holistically solve the e-waste menace while also assisting the global economy and resource conservation. Numerous reviews on one or the other aspects of e-waste generation and its recycling: global e-waste generation and management (Awasthi and Li, 2017; Kumar et al., 2017), e-waste recycling process and methods (Islam et al., 2020), regulation and legislation (Kumar and Singh, 2013), role in the circular economy (Pini et al., 2019), impact on the environment and human health (Awasthi et al., 2016; Grant et al., 2013; Vaccari et al., 2019), and sustainable management (Ravindra and Mor, 2019) have been published. However, very few of them provide a holistic picture covering most of the aspects of e-waste generation and recycling including the environmental and occupational health concern, economic and legal issues and strategies to address such issues.

This review provides a comprehensive account of the current trend in global e-waste generation, the latest approaches in e-waste recycling, environmental and occupational health concerns, opportunities and constraints in effective e-waste management, and solutions for improved e-waste recycling. Besides, we have also discussed the mechanism of toxicity of a few of the prominent pollutants associated with e-waste generation and recycling. Further, key regulations and legislative framework on e-waste management among countries generating major amount of e-waste were provided. Moreover, we have also commented on the potential strategies for improved and effective e-waste management.

2. Current status on global e-waste generation

The rate of generation of e-waste at the global level has increased substantively in recent years. While previous estimates suggested an annual growth rate of 3–4 % (ASSOCHAM-NEC, 2018; Balde et al., 2017, 2015), by the year 2019, the growth rate of global e-waste generation has increased to around 6% (Forti et al., 2020). The global e-waste generated in 2019 is estimated comprising 17.4 Mt small equipment, 13.1 Mt large equipment, 10.8 Mt temperature exchange equipment, 6.7 Mt screens and monitors, 4.7 Mt small IT and telecommunication equipment, and 0.9 Mt lamps (Forti et al., 2020). Detailed quantities of e-waste generated by individual countries in the year 2019, as well as detailed classification of EEE under above mentioned six major subheads are provided in the ‘Global E-waste Monitor 2020’ report (Forti et al., 2020). The continent-wise figures of e-waste generated during 2014–2019, and countries which generated the highest e-waste within each continent in 2019 are shown in Fig. 1. It is worth noting here that in each successive year, both total e-waste as well as per capita generation of e-waste has increased among all the continents .

Asia with its 17 countries contributed the highest share of e-waste in 2019. China, India, Japan, and Indonesia generated most of the e-waste among Asian countries. Many nations in Asia are covered by nation-based e-waste legislation which prohibit trans-boundary movement of e-waste, and mandate formal collection of generated e-waste for recycling at government-recognized setups with appropriate technology (Table 1). For a comprehensive analysis of e-waste legislation worldwide, the recent article by Patil et al. and other may be referred (Patil and Ramakrishna, 2020; Kumar et al., 2017; Pathak et al., 2017; Patil and Ramakrishna, 2020; Wei and Liu, 2012; Zeng et al., 2013) Despite various policies on e-waste management in many Asian nations, only a marginal increase in e-waste recycling at formal setups has taken place and has not kept pace with the unmatched increase in total e-waste generation . Limited coverage of EEE under e-waste management rules, lack of effective enforcement of regional and international e-waste legislation and treaties, and unprofessional standards of e-waste disposal, collection, and recycling are believed to be contributing to persisting informal recycling under sub-optimal conditions in Asian countries (Balde et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017; Wei and Liu, 2012).

Europe and Americas recorded the next highest global e-waste generation after Asian countries . North and South America have been estimated to have generated approximately 11−13 Mt e-waste annually in the past six years, with per capita contribution of approximately 12−13 kg/inhabitant per year. While European nations too maintained their total e-waste generation to around 12 Mt in the last six years; they recorded a substantial decrease in per capita generation of e-waste because of their stringent e-waste management practices. Also, the average e-waste collection and recycling through the formal system in Europe was comparatively higher (5.1 Mt) than the Americas (1.2 Mt). Most of the European nations (as part of the European Union) are covered by the EU directives to follow regulations on transparent and systematic management of generated e-waste, whereas only a few countries like the USA and Canada in the Americas have provincial laws to manage e-waste (Wang et al., 2016).

Africa and Oceania were reported to generate the least amount of e-waste in the past six years. The highest quantities of e-waste among 49 African nations analyzed for their share of e-waste was recorded from Egypt (585 kilo ton), South Africa (415 kt), Nigeria (461 kt) and Algeria (308 kt). E-waste management in Africa is still dominated by the informal sector due to the lack of either specific e-waste legislation or their implementation. In Oceania (among 12 countries analyzed for e-waste generation), Australia and New Zealand (650 kilo ton; 21.3 kg/capita) recorded generating the most of the e-waste. Most of the African and Oceanian countries either do not have e-waste management laws or schemes to solve the e-waste problem and deal with the informal recycling. However, Australia (Oceania) has enacted the National Television and Computer Recycling Scheme (2011) to increase the rate of recycling of televisions and computers to 80 % by 2026–2027 through industry-based collection and recycling initiatives (EPHC, 2010). Also, the dumping of e-waste in landfills is banned in Australia to encourage safe management of hazardous materials and increase recovery of the valuable materials.

3. Exposure to pollutants associated with e-waste: mechanism of toxicity and environmental and occupational health concerns

E-waste recycling without appropriate measures to limit environmental pollution can add a variety of organic and inorganic pollutants such as heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), brominated flame retardants (BFRs), perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins (PCDDs) and polychlorinated dibenzofurans (PCDFs) into the ecosystem which can adversely affect human health. This section discusses exposure to e-waste toxicants and mechanisms of their toxicity. Epidemiological findings highlighting health consequences in e-waste workers and population inhabiting nearby localities to sites of e-waste recycling (mostly in the informal settings) are also provided.

3.1. Exposure to e-waste pollutants

The toxic components contained in e-waste depend on the type of EEE. Besides, the emission of toxic components and their derivatives into environment is dependent of the method used for processing and recycling. Various metals and organic compounds are added to the EEE in trace quantities for various purposes, such as to impart mechanical support and strength, enhance electrical and thermal conductance, resistance to flame and weathering conditions, and other added benefits (Table S3). Being embedded in EEE, these components impose minimal adverse effects on human health when the EEE is intact. However, upon emission into the environment through recycling activities, such as dismantling, size reduction, and burning or heating these get released into the environment.

Presence of various primary e-waste toxicants (hazardous substances present in e-waste, e.g. Pb, Cd, Hg and PCBs) and secondary e-waste toxicants (produced during processing and recycling of e-waste, e.g. PAHs, dioxins and difurans) in the environment of the Guiyu town of China, Agbogbloshie of Ghana, National Capital Territory (NCT) region in India, Shershah (Karachi) in Pakistan, Lagos in Nigeria, and Dhaka in Bangladesh (all well-known e-waste dump yards) has been widely reported (RajyaSabha, 2011; Sthiannopkao and Wong, 2013). For instance, Seelampur and Mandoli industrial area in Delhi, India have been reported for contamination of drains and surface soil from discarded acid wastes that carry unrecovered metals like Sb, Cu, Pb, Ni, Sn, Zn, As and Se (Brigden et al., 2005; Pradhan and Kumar, 2014). Similarly, high concentrations of polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) and tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) have been detected in the indoor dust from TV dismantling workshops in east China and Vietnam (Anh et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2014a; Wang et al., 2010b). Presence of PBDE, particularly the BDE-47 and BDE-99, and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) has been found in soil sediments of Dayan River near an electronic waste site in Qingyuan (Zheng et al., 2015). Bioaccumulation of PBDEs, especially the BDE-209 has been found in fishes collected from ponds near to e-waste recycling localities in Vietnam (Anh et al., 2017). Various low and high molecular weight PAHs such as phenanthrene, anthracene, fluoranthene, pyrene, and benzo(a)anthracene, chrysene and dibenzo(a,h)anthracene have been reported in soil and vegetations near recycling or dumping sites in South China and Nigeria (Adeyi and Oyeleke, 2017; Wang et al., 2012). Multiple studies evidenced the presence of heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants at informal e-waste recycling sites coming mainly from crude processing, such as open burning and discharge of acid bath effluents into soil, water and other habitats (Awasthi et al., 2016; Vaccari et al., 2019).

Exposure to toxic e-waste components may result from inhalation, ingestion or upon dermal contact at workplace (occupational) or through contaminated air, water, soil and food items. Workers engaged in recycling activities, elderly people, children, and pregnant women residing near e-waste recycling units are highly susceptible to adverse health effects of e-waste toxicants (Chimere May et al., 2018; Ohajinwa et al., 2019). Particularly, children and infants, owing to the possibility of in utero exposure, intense hand-to-mouth activity, high rate of breathing, frequent breast-feeding and food intake, and low rate of toxicant removal are considered the most vulnerable group for e-waste exposure (Guo et al., 2010, 2012; Xu et al., 2018, 2012).

3.2. Mechanism of e-waste toxicity

While many of the environmental pollutants including those generated during e-waste recycling may have different mechanisms through which they can affect various body systems, their co-existence in the environment and simultaneous exposure to different magnitudes of dose, duration and routes make it extremely challenging to delineate their exact roles in various health conditions among exposed population. These challenges notwithstanding, significant progress has been made to uncover the possible mechanism of toxic effects of various e-waste toxicants.

3.2.1. Molecular mechanism of heavy metals toxicity

Cellular exposure to heavy metals is known to increase reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and deplete antioxidants. Multiple studies have indicated that redox active metal ions, such as Fe(II), Cu(II), Cr(VI), or As(III) upon getting oxidized by the by-products of aerobic respiration (e.g. hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and superoxide (O2−)) can initiate autoxidation driven by Fenton reaction, leading to production of highly reactive hydroxyl radical (OH) and hydroxide (OH−) (Flora et al., 2008; Thomas et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2017). These reactive oxygen species (ROS) can form additional free radicals such as thiyl radical (RS), carbon-centred radical ((R)3C) and peroxyl radical ((R)3COO) upon reacting with other cellular biomolecules and may damage cellular proteins, lipids, DNA and polysaccharides among other cellular machineries (Fig. 2) (Godwill et al., 2019; Lemire et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013).

Metal catalyzed oxidation of amino acid residues, such as histidine, arginine, lysine and proline adjacent to metal binding sites in proteins (form carbonyl derivatives) may result in loss of enzyme activity as well as protein dysfunction and degradation (Stadtman, 1993). Similarly, exchange of catalytic metals or structural metals, for example, displacement of metallic cofactor Zn(II) by Pb(II) from catalytic site of heme synthesizing enzyme δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (Jaffe et al., 2001), and substitutions of Ni(II) for cofactor Zn(II) at non-catalytic site of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase (an enzyme involved in glycolysis) (Macomber et al., 2011), and destruction of catalytic Fe–S clusters (2Fe – 2S; 3Fe – 3S; 4Fe – 4S) in proteins involved in electron transfer, enzymatic reactions, and RNA and DNA metabolism, can potentially lead to site-specific enzyme inhibition (Vernis et al., 2017; Xu and Imlay, 2012). Moreover, these metals can form disulphide bonds with sulphur atom in amino-acid residues in glutathione, L-cysteine, NAD(P)H and FADH2 due to their electron-sharing affinities, thus depleting the anti-oxidant reserves of the cell (Lemire et al., 2013). Oxidative breakdown of lipids, particularly at the methylene bridges (-CH2-) in polyunsaturated fatty acids or glycolipids by, for example Cu(II) and Cd(II) catalysed ROS can result in loss of membrane potential and integrity leading to impaired membrane function (Flora et al., 2008). Both oxidative stress mediated damage and inactivation of key proteins involved in DNA synthesis and repair are known as causative factors for metal-associated genotoxicity. Free radicals such as OH can react to nucleobases or 2-deoxyribose moiety resulting in DNA damage such as base lesions, 8-hydroxy-2-deoxyguanosine, and formation of inter-strand and intra-strand base cross-links, and DNA–protein cross-links (Cadet and Wagner, 2013). Inhibition of mismatch repair protein by metal ions or its effectors can result in propagation of unrepaired errors which may lead to mutations and cellular apoptosis (Jin et al., 2003). Also, some heavy metals such as Cr(VI) or Ga(III) are known to starve the cells of essential micronutrients, e.g. sulphate and Fe by interfering in their uptake through various mechanism (Lemire et al., 2013). Exposure to heavy metals has also been shown to result in neurological and behavioural disorders, diseases of nervous, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, reproductive, and immune systems, and cancers of the bladder and lungs (Jarup, 2003; Rebelo and Caldas, 2016; Rehman et al., 2018; Song and Li, 2015).

3.2.2. Molecular mechanism of PAH and dioxins toxicity

PAHs and dioxins are produced as by-products during combustion of e-waste components. PAHs are lipophilic in nature, and enter pulmonary cells via passive diffusion upon inhalation or ingestion. They activate cytochrome P450 (CYP) monooxygenases, like CYP1A1/2 and CYP1B1, and cellular enzymes such as glutathione S-transferases, UDP glucuronyl transferases, NADPH quinone oxidoreductases (NQOs), aldo-keto reductases (AKRs), and epoxide hydrolases (EHs) through aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR)-dependent and AhR-independent pathways including mainly the CYP1A1/1B1 and epoxide hydrolase pathway (CYP/EH), CYP peroxidase pathway (CYPP), and aldo-keto reductases pathway (AKR) (Moorthy et al., 2015). During this process, the PAHs are transformed to its active carcinogenic metabolites like diol-epoxides, radical cations, and reactive and redox-active o-quinones which may react with DNA to produce DNA adducts that can lead to DNA mutation, abnormal gene expression, and tumorigenesis (Fig. 3) (Moorthy et al., 2015). The toxicity due to PAH exposure is further enhanced by the metabolic processes which generate reactive metabolites such as epoxides and dihydrodiols (Burchiel and Luster, 2001; Moorthy et al., 2015). Such metabolites cause DNA adduct formation and may lead to mutations apart from protein adduct formation (Burchiel and Luster, 2001). Besides, exposure to PAHs has been found to cause oxidative stress leading to oxidative damage to DNA, oxidation of proteins, lipid peroxidation and membrane damage (Deng et al., 2014b). Chronic exposure to PAHs, in ecological settings, has been found to be associated with reduction in immune function, liver and kidney damage, retarded lung function and enhanced risk of cancers of various organs viz. lung, skin, bladder, and gastro-intestine (Armstrong et al., 2004; Bostrom et al., 2002; Burchiel and Luster, 2001; Kim et al., 2013).

Toxic effects of the dioxins appear to be mediated via genomic and non-genomic pathways by binding to the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). Dioxins entering the cells via diffusion can bind the cytosolic AhR complexed to chaperone proteins Hsp90-p23-XAP2 (heat shock protein 90, prostaglandin E synthase 3, and the immunophilin-like protein – hepatitis B virus X-associated protein 2) leading to dissociation and translocation of AhR-dioxin complex into the nucleus where it recruits AhR nuclear translocator, transcriptional proteins, co-activators and co-repressors to bind the promoter regions (xenobiotics response elements) of target genes to exhibit altered expressions (Fig. 3) (Beischlag and Perdew, 2005; Beischlag et al., 2004; Petrulis and Perdew, 2002). The rapid effects of dioxins, such as TCDD-induced inflammation appear to stem from its non-genomic action involving ligand activated AhR causing rapid rise in intracellular Ca2+ and activating protein kinases and phosphatases, for example epidermal growth factor receptor (Matsumura, 2009). Besides, hijacking of AhR by dioxins disrupts the endogenous functions such as regulation of cell-cycle, hematopoietic cell populations, tumour suppression, aging, hypoxia, and circadian rhythms (Carlson and Perdew, 2002; Marlowe and Puga, 2005; Singh et al., 2009). Chronic exposure to dioxins has also been shown to cause reproductive toxicity (interfere with hormonal signalling, anti-estrogenic effects, vitamin A inhibition, thyroxin mimicry), neurotoxicity (endocrine-disrupting actions, neural-disrupting action), immunotoxicity (immune-suppression, promotes inflammatory responses), tumorigenesis promotion etc. (Kogevinas, 2001; Marshall and Kerkvliet, 2010).

3.3. Health consequences of e-waste exposure

The health impact of e-waste exposure on humans has been mainly assessed through evaluating exposure and effect biomarkers, and analysis of morbidity pattern among exposed and control populations. A comprehensive account of the health implications of exposure to various toxicants associated with e-waste recycling has been provided by Grant et al. in a systematic review (Grant et al., 2013). Through assessing levels of e-waste pollutants and their derivatives in serum, blood, cord-blood, placenta, meconium etc., it has been suggested that exposure to e-waste toxicants may affect thyroid function (as evident by altered levels of serum thyroid stimulating hormone, tri-iodothyronine and tetra-iodothyronine in the exposed group), cause genotoxicity (higher DNA damage, increased micronuclei frequency and chromosomal aberrations), alter cellular expression and function (altered expression levels of metallothionein, S100 P and S110 P proteins), neonatal outcomes (low birth-weight, birth-length, gestational age, Apgar score and body-mass index), physical growth and cognitive functions (low weight, height, body-mass index and intelligence quotient), temperament and behaviour (behavioural neurological assessment score and temperament score), and lung function (low forced vital capacity) (Table 2).

4. E-waste recycling methods

In the modern era of rapid technological advances, a large amount of e-waste has been accumulated from the increased production of EEE that turn to e-waste upon the end of its useful life. Effective strategies are required both at production stage and after-use for environmentally sound management of the e-waste. Recycling is a valuable tool to control the rising heaps of e-waste; however, sub-optimal practices of recycling are contributing to increase in the levels of toxic pollutants in the ecosystem. The current global trend in e-waste management (informal processing of 82.6 % of global e-waste in 2019) has become unsustainable, and requires multifaceted approach for a holistic solution. Better understanding of e-waste collection and recycling process is an important link in this direction. This section discusses in brief the formal methods of e-waste collection and processes for recovery of valuable metals from e-waste.

E-waste recycling comprises (i) collection of e-waste, (ii) its processing, and (iii) recovery of valuable materials (Meskers et al., 2009). Collection and consolidation of the obsolete EEE is an important step that requires both public awareness as well as establishments in form of regulatory agreements, government policies and accessible collection facilities to facilitate efficient collection of household or institutional e-waste. Under formal collection, the e-waste is collected by government authorized organizations, and/or producers via municipal collection points, pick-up services, and retailers. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) norm, a take-back initiative put in place by various nations places the responsibility on the original equipment manufacturers to collect certain fraction of their sales.

Enrichment of valuable metals through removal of non-essential and non-recyclable fractions is the next step in recycling e-waste. It involves dismantling of the EEE to collect individual components. An e-waste, depending upon the type, manufacturer and the age of the equipment carries varying quantity of ferrous components (e.g. iron, steel), non-ferrous metals (e.g. silver, gold, copper, aluminium, platinum), plastics, glass, wood, rubber and other materials. These components are sorted to different batches of metals, plastics, ceramics, paper, wood and categories like capacitors, batteries, LCDs, PCBs to shred them into further small pieces (e.g. 0.177 mm to 5 cm) using mechanical processes (Cui and Forssberg, 2003). Industrial scale granulation machines are used for these purposes (Fig. 4). The processed e-waste is enriched for recovery by finally separating them into metallic and non-metallic fractions using magnetic, current-based, or density separation techniques (Li et al., 2007; Zhang and Forssberg, 1997).The plastic part of e-waste is mostly recycled as energy source, and to convert into plastic bottles.

Metals from the processed e-waste are recovered using hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical methods. The hydrometallurgical methods of metal recovery from e-waste use solvent extraction, leaching, adsorption and ion exchange processes for selective dissolution of precious metals, and recovery through electro refining or chemical reduction process (Ritcey, 2006; Sadegh Safarzadeh et al., 2007). Various mineral acids and oxidants including aqua-regia (3HCl:HNO3), HCl, H2SO4, HNO3/H2O2, HClO4, NaClO and lixiviants including cyanide, thiosulfate, thiourea and halide have been used for the recovery of pure base and precious metals from e-waste (Ding et al., 2019; Islam et al., 2020). Hydrometallurgical processes use toxic, highly acidic/alkaline, or flammable reagents and also generate voluminous solid wastes and effluents. Hydrometallurgy require off-gas treatment as the halogenated flame retardants used in printed circuit boards forms toxic dioxin, furans and volatile metals (Hageluken, 2006). However, it is not possible to achieve simultaneously both the inexpensive extraction and minimal emission of toxic components into the environment along with high extraction efficiency, and recyclability using any single process. Methods such as landfilling and incineration are used for treatment of effluent and other dangerous waste to minimize environmental contamination from disposed waste.

Pyrometallurgical methods of metal reclamation from e-waste involves thermal treatment of e-waste through conflagration, smelting in furnaces or alkali chemicals, drossing, sintering, plasma melting and other solid-liquid-gas reactions at high temperature for recovery of valuable metals (Antrekowitsch et al., 2006; Cui and Zhang, 2008; Ding et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019). Majority of e-waste recycling especially for Pb, Cu, and precious metals at industrial scale is performed using pyrometallurgic methods in Cu and Pb smelters (Antrekowitsch et al., 2006). These methods rely on chemical and metallurgic proportion of metals to segregate them pinto solvent metal phase (molten bath) for partial or full recovery through subsequent hydrometallurgical, electrochemical techniques. Mostly, copper smelters are used for these purposes. Separated precious metals as anode slimes are recovered through electro- or hydro-metallurgical process. Non-recyclable materials like plastics are used as energy sources (Cui and Zhang, 2008; van Schaik and Reuter, 2014). Pyrometallurgy methods are often used for initial segregation and upgrading of precious metals into base metals followed by hydrometallurgical and electrometallurgical process for the recovery of pure base and precious metals. For example, recovery of platinum group metals [e.g., Ruthenium (Ru), Rhodium (Rh), Platinum (Pt), and Palladium (Pd)] from e-waste uses a combination of hydro-, pyro- and electro- metallurgical process. Leaching into acids and separation from model solution using liquid-liquid extraction through precipitation with phosphonium quaternary salts and pH change, and ionic liquids have been reported for Pd, Pt, Ru and Rh metals (Mohdee et al., 2018; Rzelewska-Piekut and Regel-Rosocka, 2019). Similarly, extraction of gold (Au) by leaching it into lixiviates like thiourea, cyanide, halide or thiosulfate and separation through resin-based adsorption (1-ehylenediamine and 1-(2-aminoethyl) piperazine resins), or with aqueous polyethylene glycol-(NH4)2SO4 two-phase system have been reported (Bulgariu and Bulgariu, 2011; Cyganowski et al., 2017). Further details on sustainable approaches to recover precious metals from e-waste using various chemical and biological processes have been discussed elsewhere (Ding et al., 2019; Islam et al., 2020; Khaliq et al., 2014).

5. Challenges and opportunities associated with e-waste management

Metals, plastics, glass, and rare earth elements present in e-waste are valuable secondary resources. The richness of e-waste for valuable elements can be understood by estimates that suggest a typical cathode-ray tube TV carry approximately 450 g Cu, 227 g Al and 5.6 g Au (Zeng et al., 2018). Similarly, a metric ton of waste personal computers may generate more gold than that recovered from 17 metric ton of gold ore (Bleiwas and Kelly, 2001). The conventional e-waste recycling activities have, however, targeted mainly for recovering useful and easily extractable materials such as metals that are present in relatively high content and extractable forms (Baccini and Brunner, 2012). Notwithstanding the challenges in effective e-waste management, recycling e-waste have benefitted both the environment and human health (Table 3).

5.1. Major challenges in effective management of e-waste

Electronic components such as printed circuit boards, graphic and memory cards, hard drives, and cables and connector which are commonly used in gadgets like personal computers and smartphones have been the preferred sources for extraction of precious and rare earth metals (Bleiwas and Kelly, 2001). However, e-waste is not only a source of valuable materials, but also of a variety of toxic chemicals emitted during its processing and recycling. For instance, hazardous substances present in e-waste (Pb, Hg, As, Cd, PCBs; primary emission), or those produced as by-products during processing and recycling (dioxins and furans, PAHs; secondary emission) are of great concern for environment as well as human health (Orlins and Guan, 2016). A holistic approach that encompasses collection of all categories of e-waste upon end of useful life and recycle them entirely, so that no materials get wasted, is required for sustainable e-waste management (Reuter et al., 2013; Song et al., 2015).

The main challenge for managing e-waste is its massively high volume and complexity. As presented in Fig. 1, e-waste generation is increasing constantly with an estimated rate of 2 Mt annually, where China, USA, India, Japan, and Brazil together generated 50 % of the total e-waste in 2019 (Forti et al., 2020). Escalating e-waste amount is a serious concern in countries such as China and India which are leading e-waste generators as well as importers of e-waste from across the world (Wang et al., 2016). Compounded with the difficulty in separating e-waste components (i.e., some components may be bolted, others screwed, snapped, glued or soldered together), the household tendency to dispose all categories of e-waste together make it further difficult to segregate e-waste components into multiple categories such as metals, plastics, and glasses for their effective product-specific recycling (Chi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017).

Lack of environmental awareness and knowledge on e-waste disposal and collection options among households due to insufficient efforts taken by local governments to popularize e-waste recycling policies and collection strategies after implementation of relevant legislation constrain the households to either sell e-waste to peddlers or itinerant collectors, or dump as solid waste (Wang et al., 2017). Further, the lack of effective collection mechanisms and networks has promoted informal setups that could recycle only selective e-waste materials due to lack of infrastructure and technology-driven methods. As a result, high volume of valuable secondary resource is either lost, and/or multiple toxic materials from primary, secondary and tertiary emissions are released into the environment.

Lack of financial support to highly automated and technically sound formal sectors to meet high running costs for systematic e-waste collection and treatment, site rent and skilled manpower costs have restricted the role of formal systems vis-a-vis the informal sector in e-waste recycling (Lundgren, 2012). Hence, a major fraction of the e-waste is handled by informal sector at inappropriate setups which lack basic infrastructure and technology to recover all the valuable substances and are usually not able to put in place measures to prevent the escape of pollutants into the environment. The crude recycling methods adopted by informal sectors are expected to release toxic additives and hazardous substances contained or produced from e-waste treatment into the environment, posing significant threat to the environment and human health. Further, prevalence of extensive manual dismantling, for example, use of hammers, chisels and screw drivers operated with bare hands to dismantle and separate e-waste components (Puckett et al., 2002, Wen et al., 2006), and recovering metals from cables, printed circuit boards and other components via heating over coal-fired grills, burning in open air, or stripping in open-pit acid baths are key constraints to effective management of e-waste (Awasthi and Li, 2017; Chi et al., 2011; Wong et al., 2007).

5.2. Key opportunities in effective e-waste management

Despite many challenges, e-waste recycling offers multiple opportunities owing to its huge richness of resources and its role in limiting the pace of e-waste generation. The most remarkable benefit of a systematically managed e-waste recycling is that it provides a controlled processing system for the e-waste that would otherwise end up in landfills or incinerator contaminating the environment (Song et al., 2015; Widmer et al., 2005). This way, it loops the conventional linear approach of resource extraction and helps in retaining materials in use for a longer time (Fig. 5). This reduces waste generation and promotes use of secondary raw materials in production through material recycling (Cossu et al., 2012; Klinglmair and Fellner, 2010).

Various environmental and societal benefits are accrued by keeping the hazardous waste away from the landfills and reducing greenhouse gases emission and carbon footprint through decline in demand for new metal products (Debnath et al., 2015). Also, extracting raw materials from e-waste reduces the volumes of disposed waste, and the non-recyclable components can be used as fuels in industrial manufacturing to provide significant energy savings.

A huge economic component is attached with e-waste recycling. For instance, the cost of raw materials present in 53.6 Mt e-waste generated in 2019 is estimated to 57 billion USD (Forti et al., 2020). Thus, by strengthening collection and recycling of e-waste, the developing economies, which rely on import for several vital minerals including the copper, cobalt and nickel, can restrict the over-extraction and over-dependence on imports through e-waste reclamation and endure stability against price hikes, monopolistic and strategic behaviour by exporters. The potential of creation of additional jobs is another economic aspect of e-waste recycling industry.

Besides, one of the largest benefits that can be drawn from e-waste recycling is the reduced need of virgin mining for the extractable metals (Zeng et al., 2018). It is estimated that the stock of iron and copper iron in the geologic stores has almost depleted to its half. Hence, an immediate shift to large-scale resource recovery is required to preserve the remaining natural resources (Krook and Baas, 2013). Also, owing to the increasing global demand and declining ore grades, excavation of fine-grained and more complex ore deposits is required that can be compensated, at least to some extent, through e-waste recycling as the concentration and average grade of metals in the e-waste are usually higher than that of an ore extracted from mines (Zeng et al., 2018). Further, the environmental escape of toxic components of e-waste upon natural decomposition or through inappropriate disposal could be restricted through an automated e-waste recycling. This can reduce all major types of pollution associated with it and prevent the susceptible population from being exposed to hazardous e-waste pollutants.

6. Strategies for effective and environmentally safe e-waste management

The amount of e-waste generated around the global is continuously growing at substantial rate. While on the one hand, improper e-waste recycling without adequate safeguards can potentially threaten human health, on the other, it also provides livelihoods to countless poor workers, particularly in the developing countries. Hence, aiming to manage e-waste menace by just implementing legislative laws and empanelling channels for its organised recycling may not be sufficient. Collaborative efforts through mass awareness on harms and benefits of e-waste recycling, strengthening formal sectors, ensuring compliance to EPR and e-waste management norms, advancing product design, deriving engineering solutions, and strengthening the knowledge regarding adverse health effects through focused research are required to address the concerns associated with e-waste recycling. Some of such aspects are discussed in the succeeding paragraphs.

6.1. Improving the efficiency of e-waste recycling

Rate of e-waste collection through organized channels is very low, mainly due to lack of awareness regarding benefits and harms of e-waste recycling among consumers, as well as absence of provisions for economic incentives such as free collection, transportation and exchange benefits. Working upon these aspects would help in attracting customers to join recycling initiatives. Informal e-waste recycling, which also plays a pivotal role in solid waste management in many developing countries is also considered as environmental and occupational health hazard. Informal sectors are usually less-expensive to build and run, and have empirical know-how on e-waste disposal patterns of a city. Availability of relatively cheaper labour allows cost-effective manual collection and processing of large quantities of e-waste often with minimal infrastructure and investment. However, informal e-waste recyclers are often able to recover only selected materials of economic value (e.g., gold, silver) from some of the highly enriched sources (e.g., PCB) using improvised methods often releasing the un-extracted elements and generated pollutants in the environment. For reducing the occupational and environmental hazards from such collection and processing activity, it is necessary to bring such itinerant e-waste collectors and small-scale recyclers into the organized or a co-operative domain and ensure remunerative returns for their work. Linking the two actors (formal and informal sectors) through community-based organisation (CBO) and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) can be one of the viable models to promote efficient e-waste recycling (Baud et al., 2001; Henzler et al., 2017; StEP, 2020). For instance, the informal recyclers can be assigned with activities such as waste collection, disassembly, and segregation tasks, while allocating the deep recovery – the most concerning part in entire e-waste recycling process to the state-of–the art e-waste processing refineries. Since a major fraction of e-waste by weight comprises metal, glass and plastics which can be processed manually without causing significant environmental damage. The other constituents of e-waste that contain hazardous substances and would require appropriate facility and infrastructure for recycling may be sold to the authorised recyclers having access to advanced e-waste processing sectors. The informal operators may be provided appropriate remuneration for the e-waste collection, disassembly, and sorting activities. Multiple case studies have attempted to evaluate the effects of partnering the formal and informal sectors in e-waste recycling. In India, Green E-waste Recyclers, SWaCH, Saahas Zero Waste, E-WarDD, GIZ-Microsoft and Chintan collection and recycling companies have conducted case studies based on the intervention model as shown in Fig. 6 wherein the door-to-door collection of WEEE was predominantly maintained through informal sector workers, who were paid accordingly, and subsequent dismantling and recycling was carried out at these licensed recycling facilities (Henzler et al., 2017). These case studies elucidated the benefits of establishing partnership between the formal and informal sectors through trustworthy financial transactions to some extent. This mainstreaming of informal recyclers would expectedly reduce the unsafe recycling practices decreasing environmental pollution while enhancing overall recovery of useful material from e-waste.

The informal sector usually collects the consumer discarded WEEE through itinerant collectors, scrap dealers and illegal e-waste traders and perform manual dismantling and recycling at small-scale units using inferior methods. On the other hand, the formal sectors often collect WEEE through take-back system via dealers/retailers and channel it to licensed recyclers for mechanical dismantling and controlled processing for metal extraction. The proposed model of informal-formal partnerships excludes informal recyclers while engaging informal collectors into the mainstream (Fig. 6).

6.2. Sustainable production: changes to design and manufacturing process of electronic and electrical items to enable improved recycling

Advancing product design is another way to minimize generation of waste and related health issues. Proper control over the material chemistry and quality of the raw materials used in the manufacturing of electronic and electrical equipment can substantially reduce the need of raw materials and the quantity of hazardous waste generated upon the end-of-life of the products. The current trend in electronic markets that favour light weight, slim, and highly compact electronic gadgets also make it difficult to repair these gadgets due to miniaturization constraints. However, just as the display quality and size, processor speed and energy efficiency are marketing features for these modern electronic gadgets, recyclability should also increasingly be a priority for device manufacturers. Designing products for easier disassembly by minimizing the use of glue and thermally setting screws in plastic can be one way of boosting easier and efficient recycling. Producing sustainable devices that do not get obsolete too soon or have considerable long-life can be another way to deal with overproduction of EEE and subsequent generation of e-waste. Partnering industrialists with engineers, scientists, and e-waste recycling experts can help achieving such visions.

6.3. Sustainable recycling: adopting recycling methods releasing minimal toxicants

The traditional methods of recovering precious metals form e-waste using pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy often releases dangerous toxicants such as dioxins and acidic lixiviates which adversely impact the environment and human health. Developing alternative methods of metal recovery from e-waste, such as use of less toxic chemicals, e.g. thiosulfate instead of cyanide for Au extraction, or bioleaching using extremophilic microorganisms is one promising way to safer recycling of e-waste. Several microorganisms including bacteria (Acidithiobacillus caldus, A. thiooxidans, Pseudomonas balearica, P. ﬂuorescens) and fungi (Aspergillus niger, A. ferrooxidans, Purpureocillium lilacinum) have been reported for recovery of precious metals (Ag, Au, Co, Pd, Pt) as well as base metals (Cu, Ni, Fe, Zn) from e-waste (Table S4) (Islam et al., 2020). As the reported bioleaching methods are less efficient and require long bioleaching time, improvement in these two aspects through optimized microbial consortia is required.

6.4. Reducing occupational health hazards for workers engaged in e-waste recycling

Wearing personal facemasks may provide an immediate and short-term solution to those who seek to reduce their exposure to high levels of pollutants released in the workplace where e-waste recycling takes place. Cloth masks made of synthetic or natural cloth material worn across the mouth and nose had been a popular choice in developing countries due to its inexpensive nature and reusability. However, these masks though useful in reducing exposure to coarser particles (e.g. PM10), are only marginally beneficial in protecting against PM2.5 and finer particles which may be released during e-waste recycling, for which N95 masks are required.

6.5. Stringent e-waste recycling norms

In many countries, norms for e-waste recycling are either not in conformity with the changing times or are not enforced properly. However, considering that improper e-waste recycling in informal sectors poses significant burden to environmental and occupational health, there is a need to align norms and legislation with the changing nature of electronic and electrical equipment and the growing body of scientific literature. Besides, policies should be designed to facilitate research and development for improving e-waste processing technology so as to reduce the production and emission of toxic substances during e-waste recycling. Further, the norms and regulations should facilitate reuse of electronic and electrical equipment and minimisation of e-waste generation. With a greater focus on the quality of goods in the production phase, technical, and economic responsibility should increasingly be transferred from the Consumer to the Producer. Besides, production of hazardous substances during recycling and their safe disposal in recycled materials should also be regulated stringently. Moreover, norms and regulations for e-waste recycling should be enforced properly to ensure that environmental pollution and health effects on the people involved in the e-waste recycling process are reduced to minimum. Methods to assess the trans-boundary movement (import and export) of e-waste are needed, particularly as a part of trade codes between the countries. Methods such as placing GPS trackers in e-waste, deputing a researcher called “Person in the Port” at import port, or tagging a price threshold to shipment carrying e-waste have been used to monitor trans-boundary movement of e-waste (Balde et al., 2017).

7. Conclusion

In this age of information and communication technology, electronic and electrical devices have become almost indispensable. Owing to the fast-developing nature of the technology, many such devices become obsolete within a few years of their production. These factors, along with the growth in demand due to increasing purchasing power of people across the world, lead to the generation of enormous quantities of e-waste. While e-waste recycling is being carried out in many parts of the world to recover valuable materials present in e-waste, there are several concerns associated with it. In the developing world, which is the largest generator as well as the recycler of e-waste, a vast majority of such recycling units are in the informal sectors that usually lack advanced technology for e-waste recycling and are not able to take effective measures for mitigating environmental pollution associated with inefficient e-waste recycling. Moreover, even e-waste recycling in the organized sector poses several environmental and occupational health hazards which also partly stems from the fact that e-waste recycling technologies have not kept pace with the technological advancements in the field of production of electronic and electrical equipment.

Improved understanding of the challenges associated with implementing effective e-waste management practices, the pollutant emission patterns associated with various methods of extracting valuable minerals from e-waste, the major exposure routes and toxicological mechanism of various pollutants emitted during e-waste recycling can potentially help in devising strategies for mitigating environmental and health issues associated with e-waste recycling. Further, to effectively harness the opportunity associated with efficient e-waste management, a few additional approaches and strategies that may optimize the process of e-waste recycling should be considered. Such strategies may include: enforcing norms and regulations which are designed on the basis of scientific evidence; supporting the informal sector to ensure that the e-waste recycling norms are adhered to; and segregation of activities by the creation of a value chain wherein the less-sophisticated activities like collection and segregation of e-waste are entrusted to the unorganized sector whereas e-waste processing and recovery of the valuable components are carried out by the organized sector. Adopting sustainable methods of recycling, such as use of diverse group of microorganisms like chemolithotrophic and heterotrophic bacteria (e.g. Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans and Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans, Klebsiella pneumonia, Streptomyces erythraeus), fungi (e.g. Aspergilllus niger or Aspergillus nomius, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Cladosporium cladosporioides) and algae (e.g. Chorella vulgaris) for bioleaching of metals from e-waste and its recovery through biosorption can potentially overcome the issue of release of dangerous dioxins gases from traditional pyrometallurgy process or release of toxic acids. Besides, the production process should also be tweaked so that the recycling factor is also taken into account while designing and manufacturing the devices. Finally, there is an urgent need to develop novel technologies so as to facilitate efficient and safe e-waste recycling (Fig. 7). Advancing the bioleaching processes via developing microbial consortia for improved and efficient leaching of valuable metals from e-waste needs further research. It is hoped that the implementation of these solutions, taken together, should reduce the environmental and health hazards posed by inefficient and improper recycling of new generation of e-waste and should help in effective recovery of the valuable materials from the e-waste.
